ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethical approval for this study was obtained from the University of Sussex Ethics Committee (ER/MHHE20/1).
649 Ethical approval for this study was obtained from the 650 School of Psychology Ethics Committee at the University 651 of Sussex (ER/EB672/2).

The initial sample comprised 1,067 participants recruited via multiple channels, including university research participatory schemes, social media platforms, university classrooms, and snowball sampling.

Eight participants were removed if they showed no variation in arousal ratings across trials, and four because they displayed a salient negative correlation between arousal and enticement alongside lower arousal ratings for erotic compared to neutral stimuli, suggesting a possible misunderstanding of response scales direction.
Participants were primarily from the United Kingdom (28.23%), Italy (18.72%), the United States (14.33%), and Colombia (11.06%), with the remaining 27.66% distributed across other countries.

Participants were first 266 presented with a cover story introducing the goal of the study 267 as a validation of a new image-generation algorithm trained 268 to produce high-quality erotic (and also non-erotic) content.
269 Participants were informed that they would be shown a series 270 of images (presented for 2.5 s)" some of which were gener-271 ated by the algorithm and others that were real photographs.

In order to measure a proxy of the "beliefs" of participants about our manipulation and about the stimuli's nature, we devised a second phase of the experiment in which participants were asked to rate the realism of the images.
Finally, participants were debriefed 348 and were informed of the true purpose of the study, and of 349 the fact that all images were actually genuine pictures.

Finally, to obtain a more direct measure of beliefs, Phase 2 was reframed as a "pseudo-reveal": participants were told that, while the images were indeed a mix of photographs and AIgenerated images, the labels had been assigned at random, and were asked to identify which images they believed to be AI-generated.
621 Materials and Methods 622 Participants 623 The initial sample comprised 279 participants recruited 624 via Prolific©.
Inclusion criteria required participants to be 625 native English speakers or residents of countries with high 626 levels of English proficiency.
An ad-634 ditional five participants were excluded for completing the 635 study on a mobile device.
56.32% of 646 participants were from the United Kingdom, 26.82% from 647 South Africa, 10.34% from the United States, and the re-648 maining 6.51% were from other countries.

Participants were then informed that they would be shown a series of highly realistic AI-generated erotic images intermixed with real photographs, each preceded by a cue (as in Study 1) presented for 1s.

After viewing all images, participants completed a brief feedback asking them to indicate whether they found some or no images particularly arousing, and whether AI-generated images were more or less arousing than the photographs.

Participants were also asked whether differences between AIgenerated and real images were obvious or subtle, whether they perceived any inconsistencies or reversals in the labeling, and whether they believed all images were either photos or AI-generated.

Participants were then 721 asked to judge the true category of each image by indicating 722 their confidence (i.e., "Indicate your confidence that the im-723 age is fake or real") on a continuous scale from AI-Generated 724 (-3) to Photograph (3).
Following completion of phase 2, participants provided 726 general feedback regarding their experience and any addi-727 tional comments.
Finally, participants were presented with 728 a debrief page informing them that all images were, in fact, 729 real photographs.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 10 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: editor settings (3), R history (6), temporary files (1). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 659 columns across 18 data files.
#### Issues Identified

43 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 18 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: The initial sample comprised 1,067 participants recruited via multiple channels, including university research participatory schemes, social media platforms, university classrooms, and snowball sampling.

Eight participants were removed if they showed no variation in arousal ratings across trials, and four because they displayed a salient negative correlation between arousal and enticement alongside lower arousal ratings for erotic compared to neutral stimuli, suggesting a possible misunderstanding of response scales direction.
Participants were primarily from the United Kingdom (28.23%), Italy (18.72%), the United States (14.33%), and Colombia (11.06%), with the remaining 27.66% distributed across other countries.

Participants were first 266 presented with a cover story introducing the goal of the study 267 as a validation of a new image-generation algorithm trained 268 to produce high-quality erotic (and also non-erotic) content.
269 Participants were informed that they would be shown a series 270 of images (presented for 2.5 s)" some of which were gener-271 ated by the algorithm and others that were real photographs.

In order to measure a proxy of the "beliefs" of participants about our manipulation and about the stimuli's nature, we devised a second phase of the experiment in which participants were asked to rate the realism of the images.
Finally, participants were debriefed 348 and were informed of the true purpose of the study, and of 349 the fact that all images were actually genuine pictures.

Finally, to obtain a more direct measure of beliefs, Phase 2 was reframed as a "pseudo-reveal": participants were told that, while the images were indeed a mix of photographs and AIgenerated images, the labels had been assigned at random, and were asked to identify which images they believed to be AI-generated.
621 Materials and Methods 622 Participants 623 The initial sample comprised 279 participants recruited 624 via Prolific©.
Inclusion criteria required participants to be 625 native English speakers or residents of countries with high 626 levels of English proficiency.
An ad-634 ditional five participants were excluded for completing the 635 study on a mobile device.
56.32% of 646 participants were from the United Kingdom, 26.82% from 647 South Africa, 10.34% from the United States, and the re-648 maining 6.51% were from other countries.

Participants were then informed that they would be shown a series of highly realistic AI-generated erotic images intermixed with real photographs, each preceded by a cue (as in Study 1) presented for 1s.

After viewing all images, participants completed a brief feedback asking them to indicate whether they found some or no images particularly arousing, and whether AI-generated images were more or less arousing than the photographs.

Participants were also asked whether differences between AIgenerated and real images were obvious or subtle, whether they perceived any inconsistencies or reversals in the labeling, and whether they believed all images were either photos or AI-generated.

Participants were then 721 asked to judge the true category of each image by indicating 722 their confidence (i.e., "Indicate your confidence that the im-723 age is fake or real") on a continuous scale from AI-Generated 724 (-3) to Photograph (3).
Following completion of phase 2, participants provided 726 general feedback regarding their experience and any addi-727 tional comments.
Finally, participants were presented with 728 a debrief page informing them that all images were, in fact, 729 real photographs.

**Undefined-variable errors**

**3 scripts failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

**`setwd()` in the code**

**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "combine_models.R", "setwd() removed" = 1L, 
    "Path(s) it set" = "/mnt/lustre/users/psych/asf25/fictionero/models/"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

### Python code
This module also assesses whether the paper's Python code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 2 Python code files.
#### Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first) and numeric filename prefixes. Python has no `source()`-equivalent import-based ordering signal (an `import` loads a module, not the paper's own analysis flow), so that basis never applies here.

```{r}
#| echo: false

), class = "data.frame")
```

#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The Python code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 0 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. text.text: The proliferation of AI-generated content raises the question of whether beliefs about a stimulus's origin alter emotional responses to it.

Across two studies, we conceptually replicated and extended Marini et al. (2024) by presenting heterosexual participants (Study 1: N = 705; Study 2: N = 261) with erotic (Studies 1 and 2) and non-erotic (Study 1) images from validated databases (NAPS and NAPS ERO).
text.formatted: Across two studies, we conceptually replicated and extended <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Marini et al. (2024)</ref> by presenting heterosexual participants (Study 1: N = 705; Study 2: N = 261) with erotic (Studies 1 and 2) and non-erotic (Study 1) images from validated databases (NAPS and NAPS ERO).

text.text: Unbeknownst to participants, all stimuli were real photographs, each randomly labelled as "Photograph" or "AI-generated".
Participants rated sexual arousal, enticement, and valence for each image, and later judged their agreement with the labels.
Images labelled as AI-generated received lower affective ratings, but this effect was small and driven primarily by male participants.
Gender differences were robust yet contextdependent: males yielded more robust differences, partially driven by a higher baseline arousal response.
However, image of couples (Study 2), that females rated as more arousing, narrowed the gender gap found in Study 1.

Critically, the effect of the labels interacted with participant's own beliefs: photograph-labelled images were rated more arousing than AI-labelled only when participants' subsequent belief ratings were congruent with the label, and the difference between labels reversed when opposite beliefs were reported, suggesting a complex relationship between emotion and reality beliefs.
Individual-level differences in AI attitudes, pornography consumption, and sexual activity showed no reliable modulation of the labels effect.

These findings suggest that the anti-AI bias is best understood as a belief-sensitive authenticity effect rather than a uniform response to AI labels, with implications for research using synthetic stimuli and for policies mandating disclosure of AI-generated content.

Beyond their methodological interest as biologically salient stimuli for investigating the anti-AI bias, erotic stimuli are worth investigating also for their social relevance.

Indeed, genAI is often used to generate explicit visual contents (Döring et al., 2024; Lapointe et al., 2025), with an increasing number of (non-consensual) sexual deepfakes (Ajder et al., 2019; Hero, 2023).

text.text: Interestingly, the widespread consumption of explicitly AI-generated sexual content would suggest that the anti-AI bias might not generalize to erotic stimuli.
Or does it?
Easterbrook-Smith (2025) speculate that AI-generated pornography might still be valued less as it lacks the "aura of authenticity" surrounding human-made porn.

Similarly, Viola and Voto (2023) propose that, inasmuch the spread of deepfakes cast doubts about the authenticity of all media, it will end up diminishing the allure of non-consensual sexual content.

Lastly, based on previous findings that both pornography consumption and sexual activity shape affective and attentional responses to sexual content (Carvalho et al., 2018; Kunaharan et al., 2017; Prause et al., 2015; Walton & Bhullar, 2018; Youn, 2006), we explore whether the ratings of sexual stimuli is affected by either pornographic consumption or sexual activity (H5).

text.text: The initial sample comprised 1,067 participants recruited via multiple channels, including university research participatory schemes, social media platforms, university classrooms, and snowball sampling.

This strategy yielded a heterogeneous pool of both incentivised and non-incentivised individuals, including students and members of the general population from England, France, Italy, Colombia, and Spain.
Data collection occurred from the 19th of January to 1st of June 2024.
At this time, publicly available image generators such as OpenAI's DALL-E 3 (Betker et al., 2023) were producing highly photorealistic outputs.

text.text: Eight participants were removed if they showed no variation in arousal ratings across trials, and four because they displayed a salient negative correlation between arousal and enticement alongside lower arousal ratings for erotic compared to neutral stimuli, suggesting a possible misunderstanding of response scales direction.

In order to preserve homogeneous and well-powered samples, participants identifying with a gender other than Female or Male (N = 15) were excluded from further analysis, as were female and male participants reporting a sexual orientation other than Heterosexual (N = 335).
The latter comprised 150 bisexual females, 72 bisexual males, 32 homosexual females, 38 homosexual males, and 43 participants (23 females, 20 males) who reported another orientation.
The final sample consisted of 705 heterosexual participants (Mean age = 30.2 ± 11.8 years; 35.7% female).
Participants were primarily from the United Kingdom (28.23%), Italy (18.72%), the United States (14.33%), and Colombia (11.06%), with the remaining 27.66% distributed across other countries.
Ethical approval for this study was obtained from the University of Sussex Ethics Committee (ER/MHHE20/1).

265 Phase 1: Affective Evaluation.

Participants were first 266 presented with a cover story introducing the goal of the study 267 as a validation of a new image-generation algorithm trained 268 to produce high-quality erotic (and also non-erotic) content.
269 Participants were informed that they would be shown a series 270 of images (presented for 2.5 s)" some of which were gener-271 ated by the algorithm and others that were real photographs.

272 Each image would be preceded with a cue (the word "AI-273 Generated" or "Photo") presented for 1.25 s, and the par-274 ticipants' task was to rate each stimuli on several affective 275 dimensions.
276 Three analog scales were presented: Arousal ("How 277 much do you find the image sexually arousing?
This question 278 is about your own personal reaction felt in your body when 279 seeing the image"), Enticement ("How enticing and sexually 280 appealing would you rate this image to be.

Think of how 281 much, in general, people similar to you in terms of gender 282 and sexual orientation would like it"), and Valence ("Did the 283 image evoke a positive and pleasant (not necessarily sexual) 284 feeling in you, or could it be better characterized as negative 285 and unpleasant?

text.text: Items from the GAAIS formed the attitudes score (𝜔 = .72) and the rest of the items were averaged into an expectations score (𝜔 = .70).
Additionally, the first stand-alone item assesses self-reported AI knowledge on a 6-point Likert scale (Not at all -Expert).
Two items from the Consumption of Pornography Scale (COPS, Hatch et al., 2023) were included to assess pornography use frequency and duration.
An additional item assessed the recency of any sexual activity, with response options ranging from within the past 24 hours to more than a year ago.
Phase 2: Realism Beliefs.

In order to measure a proxy of the "beliefs" of participants about our manipulation and about the stimuli's nature, we devised a second phase of the experiment in which participants were asked to rate the realism of the images.
The instructions were framed as follows: "In the next phase, we would like to see if you found our image generation algorithm convincing and error-free.

We will briefly present you all the images one last time (the AI-332 generated ones, as well as the photos), and you will have to 333 rate them on how real (how realistic, photography-like) the 334 image is".
Participants then viewed the same 60 images (1 s) 335 in a newly randomised order and rated the stimuli on realism 336 with an analog slider scale (AI-generated -Photograph).
The 337 expectation was that items labelled as AI-generated would be 338 rated as less realistic than those labelled as photographs.

339 Following phase 2, a manipulation check was done by of-340 fering participants the opportunity to tick boxes pertaining 341 to their experience, including items prompting whether they 342 could distinguish which images were AI-generated or per-343 ceived no difference between photographs and AI-generated 344 images; whether they felt the AI-generated images were 345 more or less arousing; whether they believed the labels were 346 inaccurate or reversed; and whether they found some images 347 arousing or none at all.
Finally, participants were debriefed 348 and were informed of the true purpose of the study, and of 349 the fact that all images were actually genuine pictures.

As the patterns of results for the three outcomes were similar, we will focus on presenting the detailed results for Arousal as our primary outcome, and highlighting when divergent trends are present for Enticement or Valence.

To evaluate the reliability of individual-level parameters Lastly, a correlation matrix will be computed between the models' individual-level estimates and potential moderators: beliefs, attitudes towards and knowledge of AI, porn frequency and recency of sexual activity.
All analyses were conducted in R (version 4.5.2).

Betweenparticipant variability in sensitivity to the AI label was minimal, and correlations between individual-level estimates and participants' attitudes or sexual behaviour were accordingly weak and uninformative.
Beyond these findings, Study 1 surfaced several limitations.

First, participant feedback indicated that the manipulation was not fully convincing (41.7% reported disbelieving the labels), which together with the small size of the labelling effect and the minimal between-participant variability in label sensitivity, suggests that the manipulation may not have been sufficiently strong or salient, and that the cover story could be strengthened.

Second, the realism ratings of Phase 2 are an imperfect proxy for participants' beliefs about image origin, as it is arguably possible to find an image highly realistic while still believing it to be AI-generated.
Third, feedback suggested that the non-erotic images were experienced as distracting.

Moreover, presenting identical material to all participants meant that male participants viewed erotic images of males, which they rated as strongly negative, introducing a type of valenced experience with no equivalent for female participants and complicating interpretation.

Finally, the stimuli did not include depictions of couples, as multi-person images were notably difficult to generate realistically at the time, and their inclusion could have made the cover story suspicious.
Given women's greater sensitivity to relational cues, this absence of relational context may have contributed to the lower arousal ratings among female participants.
The goal of Study 2 was to replicate the main findings of Study 1 with a refined paradigm addressing the limitations identified above.

Regarding the stimuli, as the limitations in genAI realism that had prevented the inclusion of couple images had largely faded by the time of Study 2, couple-based stimuli were included to assess whether the absence of relational context contributed to the lower arousal ratings among female participants.

Additionally, non-erotic images were removed, and erotic stimuli depicting individuals were tailored to participants' gender (images of females for male participants and vice versa), alongside a fixed set of couple images presented to all participants.

Regarding the manipulation, Study 2 employed a more elaborate cover story to strengthen its credibility, framing the task as a collaboration with a (fictional) AI startup and including visual details about how AI generation works.

Finally, to obtain a more direct measure of beliefs, Phase 2 was reframed as a "pseudo-reveal": participants were told that, while the images were indeed a mix of photographs and AIgenerated images, the labels had been assigned at random, and were asked to identify which images they believed to be AI-generated.
This reframing allowed for a more direct 606 measure of beliefs without compromising the true nature of 607 the experiment (the fact that all images were actually real 608 photographs).
Based on these aims, we tested the following hypotheses.
610 As in Study 1, we hypothesised that images labelled as AI-611 generated would be rated lower in arousal than those labelled 612 as photographs (H1).
We also hypothesised that the inclu-613 sion of couple-based stimuli would narrow the gender gap 614 in arousal observed in Study 1 (H2).
Given the interaction 615 effect with Realism ratings in Study 1, we hypothesised that 616 this pattern would be even stronger, based on our improved 617 measure of beliefs (H3).
Finally, as in the previous study, we 618 tested whether attitudes towards AI (H4) and sexual activity 619 and pornographic consumption (H5) moderate responses to 620 the stimuli.

text.text: Unlike Study 1, no non-erotic images were included.
Each participant viewed 50 images relevant to their gender and sexual orientation: 25 depicting individuals and 25 depicting opposite-sex couples.
For the female-individual and male-individual categories, all 25 available NAPS ERO images were used.

For opposite-sex couples, we selected the 25 (of 50 available) with the highest arousal summed across heterosexual men's and women's normative ratings; among three images tied at the selection threshold, the one with the lowest summed valence was excluded.

After viewing all images, participants completed a brief feedback asking them to indicate whether they found some or no images particularly arousing, and whether AI-generated images were more or less arousing than the photographs.

Participants were also asked whether differences between AIgenerated and real images were obvious or subtle, whether they perceived any inconsistencies or reversals in the labeling, and whether they believed all images were either photos or AI-generated.

If participants indicated that they believed all images were either real or AI-generated, they were further asked to rate their confidence in this judgment on a scale from "Not at all" to "Completely certain".
The questionnaires used in Study 2 were largely the same as those in Study 1, with minor modifications.
In the BAIT scale, two items, assessing beliefs that AI might take control of people and interest in using AI systems in daily life, were removed.

Three items assessing AI expertise were added (e.g., "I consider myself an expert in AI technology"), as well as four items assessing one's ability to discriminate between AI and real stimuli (e.g., "I can easily distinguish between real and AI-generated images").
Lastly, 7 items assessing AI-bias were further included (e.g., "Human creators bring a unique perspective that AI cannot replicate").
This version of the BAIT resulted in 5 dimensions: Expectations (𝜔 = .76), Attitudes (𝜔 = .78), Expertise (𝜔 = .77), Discrimination (𝜔 = .80) and Bias (𝜔 = .77).
Items were rated in a 7 Likert scale from 0 (Disagree) to 6 (Agree).
Additionally, the wording was streamlined by replacing "Artificial Intelligence" with "AI" throughout the scale.

To examine whether participants' explicit beliefs about AI-generated content corresponded to their affective responses, Bayesian independent-samples t-tests compared the difference scores between images labelled as AI-generated and as photographs as a function of whether participants reported finding AI images less arousing.

For arousal, participants who reported finding AI images less arousing showed a numerically larger difference between images labelled as AI-generated and as photographs (M difference = -0.03) than those who did not (M difference = -0.009), but there was no credible evidence for a group difference (BF10 = 0.47; median 𝛿 = 0.24, 95% CI [-0.18, 0.66], pd = 88.4%).
Similarly, no credible group differences emerged for enticement or valence.

The addition of image type (i.e., images of couples vs. images of individuals) revealed a credible gender difference in ratings of individual images, with males rating them higher in arousal than females (Δ = 0.17, 95% CI [0.11, 0.22], pd = 100%).
No credible differences between males and females were found for ratings of couple images (Δ = 0.009, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.04], pd = 69.92%).

903 A key aim of Study 2 was to examine whether the in-904 clusion of relational context (i.e., via couple-based stimuli) 905 would narrow the gender gap in arousal observed in Study 1 906 (H2).
The findings partially support this prediction.
Specif-907 ically, males and females did not differ credibly in their rat-908 ings of couple images, whereas males continued to rate indi-909 vidual images as more arousing than females.

However, this 910 convergence did not arise solely from the predicted mecha-911 nism of selectively increased female arousal: females rated 912 couple images higher in arousal than images of individuals, 913 but males rated couple images credibly lower than images As per H3, under congruent trials, images labelled as photographs were rated as more arousing, enticing, and positively valenced compared to those labelled as AI-generated.
Under incongruent trials, this pattern reversed for males, consistent with the crossover effect observed in Study 1.

For females, however, no credible reversal emerged under incongruent trials, indicating an absence of the predicted effect rather than merely a weaker version of it; some credible differences did emerge for females under congruent trials for enticement and valence ratings.
Thus, while the predicted crossover interaction was observed, support was essentially confined to male participants, only partially replicating Study 1.
The overall effect of AI labelling remained small and showed minimal reliable variability across participants, replicating the pattern observed in Study 1.
Consequently, as in Study 1, it was not possible to draw strong conclusions regarding individual differences as moderators of the labelling effect (H4-H5).
Weak associations were found between arousal responses (both baseline and AI-related parameters) and self-reported beliefs, attitudes, and AI expertise (see full analysis on the link provided above).
The present paper investigated the anti-AI bias in response to erotic stimuli across two studies.

Overall, the findings provide converging evidence for three main conclusions: (1) there is a consistent but small effect of AI labelling on responses that is primarily observed in males, (2) there is a strong gender difference in response to erotic stimuli, that is robust and context dependent, and (3) belief-related processes (i.e., congruency between initial labels and subsequent realism/reality judgements) play a central role in shaping affective responses.
In line with previous findings (e.g., Marini et al., 2024), images labelled as AI-generated were generally rated as less arousing than those labelled as photographs.
text.formatted: In line with previous findings (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Marini et al., 2024)</ref>, images labelled as AI-generated were generally rated as less arousing than those labelled as photographs.

text.text: However, across both studies this effect was small in magnitude and primarily driven by male participants, whose ratings were higher in arousal, enticement, and valence, for images labeled as photographs than for those labeled as AI-generated.
On the contrary, in Study 1, females rated relevant erotic images higher in arousal (but not valence or enticement) when they were presented as AI-generated.
This reverse pattern was not found in Study 2.
Our results also replicate and extend prior literature on gender differences in response to erotic stimuli (Chivers et al., 2004; Chivers, 2017; Huberman et al., 2015; Safron et al., 2020).

text.text: However, their perceived origin must be controlled.

Researchers using AI-generated erotic, affective, or social stimuli should therefore measure, manipulate, or report participants' beliefs about stimulus authenticity, rather than assuming that visual realism alone makes synthetic and photographic stimuli psychologically interchangeable.

Our results also corroborate the hypothesis that the 'authenticity aura' might indeed enhance the appeal of sexual content perceived to be 'genuine' over AI-generated content (Easterbrook-Smith, 2025).

text.text: This might yield ambivalent effects.

On the one hand, the general skepticism about content authenticity in the face of the rise of AI-generated content might dampen the incentives to spread non-consensual sexual material, as proposed by Viola and Voto (2023).

text.text: On the other hand, this reduced affective reaction might translate into a 'moral discounting' and actually promote the spread of such content, based on the (false) assumption that explicitly fake non-consensual sexual deepfakes are not harmful (see Flynn et al., 2022).
text.formatted: On the other hand, this reduced affective reaction might translate into a 'moral discounting' and actually promote the spread of such content, based on the (false) assumption that explicitly fake non-consensual sexual deepfakes are not harmful (see <ref type="bibr">Flynn et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: A final consideration pertains to the possible impact of disclosing deepfakes of sensual (though not necessarily sexual) pictures depicting human bodies in a wider societal context.
Recall that some legislation, notably the recent EU AI Act (Art. 50), will soon mandate the explicit disclosure of the AI-generated origin of some media.

An unexpected effect of such legislation when it comes, for instance, to advertising perfume or swimwear, might be that AI-generated models, while explicitly flagged as such, could lose some of their allure with respect to their human counterparts.
Interpreting the results of this study requires particular caution due to the nuance of its design.

As expressed above, it is worth recalling that a substantial proportion of participants expressed doubts about the manipulation (in Study 1, 41.7% reported disbelieving the labels; in Study 2, 32% believed all images were real), meaning the experimental manipulation was not fully convincing for a meaningful portion of the sample.
We contend, however, that this limitation extends to all similar studies, stressing the relevance of including explicit attention checks before drawing any conclusion.
Additionally, while the present findings are consistent with a crossover effect linking arousal and perceived authenticity, the design cannot establish the direction of this relationship.
The observed congruency effects are equally consistent with authenticity impressions shaping subsequent arousal, or with arousal being retrospectively used to infer authenticity.
Resolving this ambiguity would require designs capable of manipulating, rather than only measuring, one of these two processes.
Moreover, future studies are needed to establish whether these effects extend to nonheterosexual samples.
To summarise, we investigated the anti-AI bias for erotic stimuli by conceptually replicating Marini et al. (2024).

In this context, reliability refers to cases in which variability between groups (e.g., participants) exceeds the uncertainty in the estimates, suggesting the presence of meaningful inter-individual differences.

After collecting subjective ratings of arousal, 517 enticement and valence for each image, we assessed the effi-518 cacy of the labelling manipulation by asking participants to 519 rate how realistic they deemed each image.

Study 2, which presented only relevant stimuli, exam-969 ined whether the gender gap in arousal observed in Study 1 970 was contingent on the nature of the stimuli.

When relational 971 context was introduced through couple-based images, this 972 gap narrowed substantially: males and females did not differ 973 in their ratings of couple images, while a gap persisted for 974 images depicting individuals.
Notably, Study 2 also showed 975 that females rated images of couples higher than images 976 of individuals, while males did the opposite.

This finding 977 supports the interpretation that female sexual responses are 978 more sensitive to contextual and relational cues (Laan et al., 979 1994; Rupp & Wallen, 2007, 2009) and suggests that the 980 absence of such features in Study 1 likely amplified the ap-981 parent gender gap in affective reactions.

text.text: Third, and most importantly, the present findings high-983 light the central role of belief-related processes in shaping af-984 fective responses.
In both studies, when asked for feedback, 985 a substantial proportion of participants expressed doubts 986 about the veracity of the labels.
We further evaluated these 987 belief-related effects on ratings by operationalising a congru-988 ency variable, which revealed a crossover interaction with 989 condition.
When participants' realism judgments were con-990 gruent with the initial label, images labelled as photographs 991 were rated higher than those labelled as AI-generated.

In 992 contrast, when judgments were incongruent, this pattern re-993 versed, with AI-labelled images receiving higher ratings, 994 suggesting that participants' affective responses are closely 995 tied to whether they were second-guessing the authenticity 996 of the images.

We had additionally hypothesised that individual differ-998 ences in AI attitudes and beliefs, pornography consumption 999 frequency and recency of sexual activity might be associ-1000 ated with the strength of this labelling effect.

However, 1001 individual-level estimates of sensitivity to the AI-generated 1002 label showed minimal reliable variability between partici-1003 pants, meaning these hypotheses could not be meaningfully 1004 tested in the present data; weak correlations with these vari-1005 ables should accordingly not be read as evidence against an 1006 association, but as uninformative given the lack of reliable 1007 variance to explain.
1008 relevant implications for research using 1014 synthetic stimuli.

Attracted by the clear advantages in 1015 terms of controllability, scalability, and stimulus standard-1016 ization, several researchers are promoting the use of AI-1017 generated stimuli in psychological research (Albohn et al., 1018 2022;

Across both studies, AI labelling produced consistent but 1075 small effects, driven primarily by male participants, along-1076 side robust gender differences in responses to erotic stimuli 1077 that proved sensitive to relational context.

Most importantly, 1078 affective responses depended on whether participants be-1079 lieved the labels: when realism judgements were congruent 1080 with the assigned label, images labelled as photographs were 1081 rated as more arousing than those labelled as AI-generated, 1082 whereas this pattern reversed when the labels were disbe-1083 lieved.

Individual differences in AI attitudes, pornography 1084 consumption, and sexual activity could not account for the la-1085 belling effect, as sensitivity to the AI label showed little reli-1086 able variability across participants.

Together, these findings 1087 suggest that the anti-AI bias is best understood not as a uni-1088 form response to AI labels but as a belief-sensitive authen-1089 ticity effect, one with practical implications for researchers 1090 using synthetic stimuli and for policies mandating the disclo-1091 sure of AI-generated content.
